title: Effects of human disturbance on five-lined skink (Eumeces fasciatus) abundance and distribution at Point Pelee National Park, Canada

authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology, University of Guelph, Guelph, ON, N1G 2W1

Department of Biological Sciences, University of Windsor, Windsor, ON, N9B 3P4

abstract_text: The five-lined skink is widely distributed in eastern North America but its populations are disjunct and of conservation concern in the northern portion of its range. Canadian populations are presently considered "vulnerable". We studied effects of human disturbance on five-lined skinks at Point Pelee National Park, from 1990 to 1997. Surveys indicated low skink abundance and a lack of woody debris in areas heavily used by humans. A population decline, concurrent with high disturbance levels, occurred from 1990 to 1996. Skinks used woody debris as refuge sites and showed preferential use of large moderately decayed logs and boards having greater surface area. Human disturbance resulted in degradation and removal of debris. To test the hypothesis that skink absence in human high-use areas was caused by a lack of suitable debris, we placed artificial microhabitats in areas which previously lacked debris and skinks. Experimental boards were quickly colonized and heavily used despite high disturbance rates. Results suggested that skinks are resilient to minor disturbances such as board displacements, but not to removal or degradation of debris. Habitat restoration by moving large woody debris from open beach to the stabilized dune began in 1996 and resulted in increased skink abundance in 1997.

title: The effects of road mortality on two threatened snake species on Pelee Island, Ontario

authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology, University of Guelph, Guelph, Ontario, N1G 2W1

abstract_text: Road mortality is becoming an increasing threat to endangered and isolated reptile populations. Reptiles killed by motorized vehicles and found on Pelee Island's roads (68 km in total) were collected and locations recorded from 1993-1996. During the three years of intense surveys, the roads were scanned approximately every two days. In 1998, sections of road that had high numbers of roadkilled blue racers (Coluber constrictor foxii) and eastern fox snakes (Elaphe gloydi) during the roadkill surveys, will be scanned intensively to determine suitable methods to mitigate the effects of vehicular mortality. The blue racer is endangered in Canada, and threatened status for the eastern fox snake is pending review. In three years 78 blue racers (11 adults/year) and greater than 100 eastern fox snakes were found dead on Pelee Island's roads. Many adult females that are killed on the roads are moving to or from shoreline oviposition sites. In the fall of each year, many hatchlings are also found dead on the roads. For example, from 1993-1996, 75 hatchling eastern fox snakes were recorded as roadkills. As a result of continuing development in the form of summer cottages, and growing tourism, vehicular traffic continues to increase on Pelee Island's roads. The future impact of increased traffic flow and continued road mortality on the blue racer and eastern fox snake remains to be seen. Our data suggest that road mortality will be a significant factor leading to the decline of both snake species on Pelee Island.

title: The impact of roads on snake populations in eastern Texas

abstract_text: Radio-telemetry studies of timber rattlesnakes (Crotalus horridus) and Louisiana pine snakes (Pituophis ruthveni) suggested that mortality associated with roads was a significant factor in the biology of these species. An analysis of timber rattlesnake records in relation to road densities supported the hypothesis that mortality associated with roads has resulted in the extirpation of this species from significant portions of the landscape. The hypothesis that existing road networks depress populations of large snake species was tested using a trapping protocol to sample snake populations up to 850 m from road corridors. Preliminary results suggest that snake populations are reduced by 50% or more up to a distance of 450 m from roads with moderate use. There was no indication that the population indices had reached an asymptote at a distance of 850 m. For some species the data suggest that larger individuals are located further from road corridors. Quantification of the road network on a landscape scale indicates that the large snake fauna of eastern Texas is subject to significant road related mortality that has the potential to reduce populations by 50% or more across a large proportion of the landscape.

title: Habitat use, home ranges and hibernacula of the copperbelly water snake (Nerodia erythrogaster neglecta) in southern Indiana and northwest Kentucky

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, Indiana-Purdue University, Ft. Wayne, IN 46805 USA
Department of Biology, Indiana-Purdue University, Ft. Wayne, IN 46805 USA

abstract_text: The copperbelly is federally listed under the Endangered Species Act as Threatened in the northern part of its range, and protected to the south by the Copperbelly Water Snake Conservation Agreement. Snakes from two populations were radio-tracked at the Sloughs Wildlife Management Area, Kentucky, and in the Patoka National Wildlife Refuge, Indiana. The movements of the snakes were monitored to elucidate patterns of home range size and habitat use, including hibernacula sites. Habitat use was seasonally compared between sexes. Home ranges and activity centers were calculated using minimum convex polygons. Individual snakes occupied widely different habitats, demonstrated pronounced fidelity to selected habitats for much of the season. Buttonbush sloughs and areas of shallow water with emergent vegetation were most frequently used, while closed canopy forested habitats away from the sloughs and large bodies of open water were not. Habitat use shifted towards palustrine forest edges as the season progressed. The hibernacula of most snakes were crayfish burrows or stumps near or within the floodplain.

title: Conservation of the endangered copperbelly water snake, Nerodia erythrogaster neglecta

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, Indiana-Purdue University, Fort Wayne, IN 46805 USA

abstract_text: The copperbelly is an inhabitant of shallow wetlands in parts of the midwestern United States. It is state listed as Endangered by Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio, federally listed as Threatened to the north by the US Fish and Wildlife Service, and protected in southern Indiana, southern Illinois, and Kentucky by a conservation agreement. Over the last few years, efforts have dramatically increased to learn more about the species' ecological requirements to prevent further losses of snakes or suitable habitat. I will review efforts to conserve the remaining populations of the copperbelly. Discussion will include a review of the current status of the snake, both in the legal and biological senses, and a description of the conservation agreement. I will also examine the implications of research findings from several studies out of my lab regarding management decisions about restoring and reclaiming habitat for the species.

title: Long-term changes in movement patterns of massasauga rattlesnakes following a severe flood

authors.affiliation: Dept. of Biological Sciences, Southeastern Louisiana Univ., Hammond, LA 70402-0736 USA
Dept. of Biological Sciences, Southeastern Louisiana Univ., Hammond, LA 70402-0736 USA

abstract_text: From 1979-1983 we conducted radiotelemetry and mark-recapture studies on massasauga rattlesnakes (Sistrurus catenatus) at the Squaw Creek National Wildlife Refuge in northwestern Missouri. These data showed that snakes hibernated in a moist prairie, moved away from the prairie to drier areas in the late spring and summer, and returned to the prairie in the fall. In 1993, the refuge was impacted severely by the 'Great Midwestern Flood'; massasauga populations showed significant changes in population size structure, sex ratio, mass-length relationships, and reproduction as a result of this event. From 1996-1997 we re-examined the movement patterns of this population to determine any additional effects of the flood. We found that although snakes still hibernate in the main prairie, very few massasaugas leave the prairie for outlying areas, but remain in the prairie during the summer. In addition, the number of massasaugas found crossing roads on the refuge has decreased dramatically, and the snakes that do cross refuge roads are mainly neonates rather than adults as was seen in the earlier study. The implications for these apparent changes in movement patterns for management and conservation will be discussed.

title: Amphibians, reptiles, and phosphate mining in Florida

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology and Center for Urban Ecology, University of South Florida, Tampa, Florida 33620, USA
Department of Biology and Center for Urban Ecology, University of South Florida, Tampa, Florida 33620, USA

abstract_text: Much of central Florida has been subjected to strip mining for phosphate. The mining process drastically alters the upland habitats available for wildlife occupancy. We collected amphibians and reptiles at 30 unmined xeric upland sites and 30 previously mined sites to determine which amphibians and reptiles may be under-represented at the reclaimed mined sites. Thirteen species of amphibians (4) and reptiles (9) were determined to be 'focal species,' that is, they were under-represented at the reclaimed mine sites, relative to the unmined sites. Reasons for their under-representation include the lack of suitable substrate for burrowing species, lack of temporary ponds for amphibian reproduction, and lack of sufficient litter, ground cover, and plant structure for other species. Plans to further study selected focal species, including translocating common species to reclaimed habitats will be reviewed.

title: Phylogeography of the anchovies (Genus Engraulis)

authors.affiliation: Northwest Fisheries Science Center, National Marine Fisheries Service, 2725 Montlake Blvd East, Seattle WA 98112 USA
Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences, University of Florida, 7922 NW 71st Street, Gainesville FL 32653 USA

abstract_text: Anchovies (genus Engraulis) inhabit temperate upwelling zones and boundary currents across the globe, including locations in Europe (E. encrasicolus), southern Africa (E. capensis), Australia (E. australis), Japan (E. japonicus), Mexico-California (E. mordax), Chile-Peru (E. ringens), and Argentina-Brazil (E. anchoita). Comparisons of mtDNA cytochrome b sequences reveal four major lineages corresponding to three New World species and a single lineage including all four Old World species. The relationships among haplotypes in the Old World anchovies demonstrate recent colonization events between Japan and Australia, and between Europe and southern Africa. A previous population in southern Africa (possibly the progenitor of the European population) may have gone extinct and been recently recolonized from Europe. A comparison of anchovies to sardines (genus Sardinops), which have a similar geographic distribution, reveals a dramatically different distribution of mtDNA lineages. These data prompt two conclusions about the biogeography of temperate marine fishes. First, a vicariance model alone is inadequate to explain the distribution of evolutionary lineages in these taxa. Both vicariance and dispersal events are strongly implicated. Second, the principle of generalized tracks, in which species with similar distributions have similar evolutionary histories, is contradicted by a comparison of phylogeographic patterns in sardines and anchovies.

title: Phylogeography of the plains killifish, Fundulus zebrinus: implications for its zoogeography and taxonomy

authors.affiliation: University of Colorado, Boulder, CO 80309-0334, USA
University of Colorado, Boulder, CO 80309-0334, USA
Colorado Division of Wildlife, CO, USA

abstract_text: The plains killifish, Fundulus zebrinus, is a smallish cyprinodontid fish found throughout the western plains states, and additionally it has been introduced to the Colorado River drainage. The widespread distribution of F. zebrinus has suggested the possible influence of historical connections among these drainages. In an attempt to describe the geographic patterns of genetic variation in F. zebrinus, we examined variation in allozymes and mitochondrial DNA (RFLP's and COI sequence). The genetic relationships among populations demonstrated a considerable degree of concordance across data sets. The geographic assemblages revealed have implications for our interpretations of the geologic history of the Great Plains. Some controversy exists as to whether there is in reality two species of Fundulus (i.e. F. kansae in the northern portion of the range). The phylogeography revealed a distinct break between northern and southern populations, suggesting that the taxonomic status of F. zebrinus might warrant closer study.

title: History and diversity of Great Basin fishes

authors.affiliation: Museum of Zoology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI 48109-1079, USA

abstract_text: Hubbs' and Miller's research on the Great Basin emphasized changes at the level of races and subspecies; these changes apparently occurred rapidly, in hundreds to thousands of years. Miocene to Pleistocene fossils of these fishes, in contrast, suggest unexpectedly slow changes at the species level, i.e., over hundreds of thousands to nearly 10 million years, with infrequent evolution of new species. Resolution of this incongruence requires clarification of the relative frequency of short-term differentiation, species origins, and extinction. The Great Basin evidence demonstrates that fluctuating pluvial-interpluvial cycles result in rapid proliferation of new subspecies, but eventual extinction of all but generalist survivors, often as relict endemics. The frequent extinctions and infrequent persistence of new species in the Great Basin seem to be the consequence of repeated loss of habitat during interpluvial stages of Pleistocene cycles. The result seems to be rapid but superficial changes in morphology without long-term change. Great Basin fish faunas exhibit low diversity and high endemism characteristic of tectonically active areas. The low diversity suggests that high extinction rates were caused by high elevations, high gradients (low habitat diversity), and climatic variability.

title: Biogeography and life history variation in flatfishes (Pleuronectidae: Pleuronectiformes)

authors.affiliation: National Marine Fisheries Service, Systematics Laboratory, MRC 153, Museum of Natural History, Washington, D.C. 20560, U.S.A.

abstract_text: Flatfishes of the family Pleuronectidae are distributed in marine waters across the entire northern hemisphere. The majority of species (49 out of 59) are found in the Pacific Ocean with only ten pleuronectid species in the Atlantic Ocean. Some species inhabit wide ranges inhabiting Pacific, Atlantic and Arctic waters, while many others have more limited distributions. An area cladogram using a recent cladistic hypothesis of relationships within Pleuronectidae allows for the interpretation of this geographic distribution. A trans-arctic dispersal appears to be a repeated pattern within taxonomic subgroups of Pleuronectidae. Associated with this extensive distribution is a wide range of life history traits. Feeding behavior, spawning season, age and size at maturity all exhibit variation at different taxonomic levels, including within species variation for some of the widely distributed species. The extent to which inheritance versus geographic distribution, and corresponding environmental factors influence these life history variables will also be presented.

title: Sangre de Cristo and other local color from Mexico: geographic variation in sexually selected characters?

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, New York University, Washington Square, NY 10003, USA
Department of Biology, New York University, Washington Square, NY 10003, USA

abstract_text: The variable platyfish, Xiphophorus variatus, has the broadest range of any species of Xiphophorus. Most work on this species has concentrated on populations in the Rio Tamesi drainage, towards the northern end of its distribution. Here, we report on the populations toward the southern end of the range, in the Rios Nautla, Solteros, Tecolutla and Cazones. These populations differ from the ones in the north by exhibiting pronounced local variation in adult male coloration patterns. One variety, termed Sangre de Cristo in the aquarium literature, is characterized by deep red coloration on the belly and throat of adult males. Another color variety is vivid yellow coloration of the gonopodium. These color variants, and others, are extremely restricted in geographic distribution. Sangre de Cristo occurs in an area no larger than ten by fifteen kilometers, with the frequency of the variant highest towards the center of the range. Yellow gonopodium is known from only a single locality. In contrast, adult male color variants in the north seem more broadly distributed. Population genetic data suggests that populations in the south may be more isolated from one another than in the north. AP-PCR (RAPD) analyses reveal less band variation in the southern populations than in the northern populations. There is also less variation at the autosomal tailspot locus in southern than in northern populations and greater tailspot variability among populations in the south. It is hypothesized that the evolution of local color variants is promoted by reduced gene flow among populations. This is of great interest because vivid adult male colors in poeciliids are generally believed to be sexually selected characters and these results suggest a potential role of small population effects in their origin.

title: A couple of case studies in African ichthyobiogeography: Anabantidae and Malapteruridae

authors.affiliation: Ichthyology Laboratory, Royal Museum of Central Africa, B-3080 Tervuren, Belgium

abstract_text: Africa has a large and diverse fish fauna which is spread across a variety of ecosystems and habitats. A preliminary synthesis of factors structuring the distributions of these fishes (exclusive of the Great Lake faunas) is attempted. Rigorous phylogenetic hypotheses are available for very few African taxa. In fact, even basic taxonomic and distribution information is lacking for many groups and regions, complicating progress in this field. This leaves most biogeographic discussions more in the realm of Humphry Greenwood's bioaccountancy than true biogeography. Many fishes seem distributed to the limits of their preferred habitats while others seemingly pay little heed to habitat boundaries, indicating more complex factors are in play. Example fish distributions from two families, Anabantidae (climbing perches) and Malapteruridae (electric catfishes), are used to explore types of distribution patterns, with possible explanations (or 'accountings') offered.

title: Fifty years of faunal change in Lake Pontchartrain

authors.affiliation: Department of Biological Sciences, University of New Orleans, New Orleans, LA, 70148 USA

abstract_text: Lake Pontchartrain, a complex, warm-temperate, shallow basin, is one of the largest estuaries in the Gulf of Mexico region. The lake is bounded by Mississippi River deltaic plain on the west and south, incised Pleistocene terraces to the north and barrier islands and older river deltas to the east. Salinity varies from pure freshwater on the western fringe of the basin to nearly marine conditions in the eastern components of the basin. Freshwater input is primarily from rivers draining the Pleistocene terraces with occasional natural (and more recently, man-made) incursions from the Mississippi River. During the last century significant degradation of the lake has occurred due to pollution, shoreline erosion, commercial shell dredging and saltwater intrusion from navigational waterways. The fauna of the lake reflects these varied hydrological connections, with well over 120 species of fish known from the basin. However, the human impact on the lake's fauna has been considerable. In order to provide an inventory of the basin and design a monitoring program to assist with lake management, the University of New Orleans has been engaged in a four year assessment of the health of the basin. Quarterly collections are made by trawl and/or seine at 15 stations approximating sites surveyed by Suttkus in the early 1950's and Thompson and Verret in the late 1970's. The first two years of the present study (1996-98) have yielded nearly 80 species of fishes with the bay anchovy most common in trawls and inland silversides most common in seine collections. In addition, we have collected nine specimens of Rio Grande perch, Cichlasoma cyanoguttatum from a variety of locales.

title: Distribution of fishes in the West Twin River drainage in relation to late-glacial events

authors.affiliation: Division of Natural Science, St. Norbert College, De Pere, WI 54115 USA

abstract_text: We assessed the occurrence of fishes upstream and downstream from a waterfall near the mouth of the Devils River, a tributary to the West Twin River in the Lake Michigan drainage of east-central Wisconsin. We hypothesized that species above the waterfall colonized the upper Devils River when the West Twin River valley served as a spillway from Glacial Lake Oshkosh to Lake Michigan, because terrace elevations indicate that the waterfall was submerged under higher flow regimes. We found eighteen native fish species above the waterfall, whereas seventeen native species occurred in the West Twin River only below the waterfall. To test the hypothesis that only relatively early colonists gained access to the upper Devils River, we assigned an independently derived ranking to each species according to its suspected timing of colonization elsewhere in the Upper Midwest. There were no significant differences between the rankings of fishes found only below and those found above the waterfall. Constraints on fish distribution imposed by geological history may be relevant to the assessment of stream ecosystem health: a stream reach above the waterfall had a lower Index of Biotic Integrity score than a similar reach below, reflecting the absence of some species above the waterfall.

title: Temporal dynamics of fish assemblages on small patch reefs: comparison of high diversity (Great Barrier Reef) and low diversity (Virgin Islands) systems

authors.affiliation: Biology & Great Lakes Institute for Environmental Research, Univ. of Windsor, Windsor, ON N9B 3P4

abstract_text: We use data from 10 visual censuses over five years of fish assemblages on small patch reefs located on the back-reef at Tague Bay, St. Croix, U.S. Virgin Islands. These are compared with comparable data from a 10-year study of southern Great Barrier Reef patch reefs. Tague Bay assemblages were substantially less diverse (total of 88 species recorded versus 141 species at the Australian site), but displayed almost the same levels of temporal variation (change in composition from census to census) as did the Australian assemblages. This result and related observations argue for the composition and dynamics of fish assemblages in the two locations to be determined by substantially similar processes. An analysis of the data, with fish classified into 12 feeding guilds rather than into species, showed variation in guild structure from census to census in both locations. However, the guild composition of Tague Bay assemblages fluctuated around a structure that was markedly different from the average structure of the Australian assemblages. While assemblages in the two locations are structured by similar processes, they play markedly different trophic roles.

title: The fish assemblages of San Diego Bay, California

authors.affiliation: California State University, Northridge, CA USA

abstract_text: Twelve quarterly samples of the fish assemblages of San Diego Bay were taken from July 1994 to April 1997 at four stations using a variety of sampling methods (large seine, small seines, square enclosure, purse seine, beam trawl and otter trawl) designed to assess all components of the ichthyofauna. These samples yielded a total of 405,034 fishes belonging to 75 species that weighed 1,725 kg. The northern anchovy was the most abundant fish species, comprising 51% of the total catch, followed by topsmelt at 22%, the slough anchovy at 13%, Pacific sardine at 3%, and shiner surfperch at about 2% of the total catch. Round stingrays constituted 22% of the total biomass taken followed by northern anchovy at 14%, spotted sand bass at about 13%, topsmelt, 10%, and slough anchovy, 6%. Marked changes in the number individuals and total biomass occurred over the course of the study. Both numerical abundance and biomass were highest in the spring and summer months due largely to heavy recruitment of juvenile surfperches and topsmelt. Very large catches of juvenile northern anchovy, Pacific sardine, round stingrays, and spotted sand bass caused the pronounced peaks in July. A similar number of fish were taken in the vegetated and non-vegetated areas, however different gears yielded varying results with respect to densities in vegetated and non-vegetated areas. According to canonical correlation analysis, distance from the mouth of the bay, temperature, and salinity accounted for nearly 95% (R2 = 0.949) of the variance in species abundances.

title: Community structure of demersal reef fishes of the Mississippi-Alabama outer continental shelf

abstract_text: Hard-bottom features of the Mississippi-Alabama outer continental shelf in the northeastern Gulf of Mexico (the Pinnacles) were surveyed to determine faunal composition and relative abundance of resident reef fishes. Study reefs of low, medium and high profile features spanning a depth range of 58 to 110 m were investigated by remote operating vehicle (ROV), trapping, trawling, and hook and line sampling. Combined sampling techniques documented ~150 species of demersal fishes, including 74 species of reef fishes. The purpose of this study is to provide a comparison of reef fish diversity to other regions of the Gulf of Mexico, and identify the trophic structure of the reef fish community.

title: Distribution patterns and physical parameters affecting Blacksmith larvae, Chromis punctipinnis, off the north west coast of Catalina Island

authors.affiliation: California State University, Northridge, Department of Biology, 18111 Nordhoff St., Northridge, Ca. 91330-8303, USA

abstract_text: Populations of damselfishes (Pomacentridae) are frequently found near kelp beds and rocky areas along open coasts. They have demersal eggs and planktonic larvae. From the time of hatching through the three stages of larval development (preflexion, flexion and post flexion) many environmental factors influence development, distribution and abundance. This investigation focuses on pomacentrid early life history stages in relation to environmental factors that influence their distribution and abundance. Four locations were selected (two inshore and two offshore) off the north west coast of Catalina Island. A one meter plankton net was towed, for five minutes, in sets of five replicates per site over a duration of three lunar cycles (200 samples). Water temperature, salinity, pH, current direction, wind velocity and lunar cycles were recorded for all tows. Data were analyzed using 3-way ANOVA. Preliminary results show increased densities inshore, with predictable cycling over the sampling period. Fluctuations in physical parameters appear to affect inshore and offshore larval distributions and abundances. This information will aid in predicting settlement for future recruitment into local populations.

title: Use of GIS in taxonomic collections and its relevance to assessing biodiversity, spatio-temporal distributions, and field work validation

authors.affiliation: F.D.E.P., Florida Marine Research Institute, 100 Eighth Ave. SE, St. Petersburg, FL 33701-5095, USA

abstract_text: A system that analyzes and displays spatially referenced data is known as a geographical information system (GIS). The use of GIS technology has facilitated understanding of complex relationships between organisms and their environment. In ichthyology, GIS could facilitate access to information associated with taxonomic collections. It could provide spatial analysis within and among species using distribution patterns of morphological and genetic characters; accurately analyze geographical distributions of morphological characters and correlate them with ecological parameters; and provide an objective measurement of the status of an ecosystem, which has generally been done based on human perception but lacked data. Taxonomic collections of voucher and type specimens and their associated environmental data are abundant sources of unexplored information. This information is highly relevant for management of natural resources because taxonomy has been built upon it. This information, when analyzed with GIS, could be used to address these areas and to provide the foundation for measuring fish biodiversity and evaluating the dynamics of spatio-temporal patterns of fish. The FDEP's FMRI is applying GIS technology to analyse the robust databases associated with its voucher collections. Further study of voucher specimens will allow us to produce maps of morphological characteristics of fish linked to ecological parameters. We also intend to produce synthesized information for ecosystem management in a format amenable to spatial- and time-analysis study.

title: Borders and biodiversity: a plight for Pacific salmon

authors.affiliation: Fisheries and Oceans Canada, Pacific Biological Station, Nanaimo, B.C.

abstract_text: If Pacific salmon are a cultural icon, then their treatment in the past century is certainly inconsistent with this value. Recent reviews of their status in Canada and the Pacific northwest report about 1,000 populations extinct or at risk, and several stocks are listed or proposed for listing under the U.S. Endangered Species Act. Causes of the declines are numerous, usually attributed to someone or something else, and always debatable. The history of impacts can be broadly characterized as: an initial uninformed and rapid expansion of fisheries; then decades of rapid economic expansion in many sectors plus heightened competitive over-fishing of hatchery and wild salmonids; and finally, 20-30 years of extensive regulation, confrontation, and change. During the latter period, the issue of "borders" in management and conservation has become very evident. The Pacific Salmon Treaty between the United States and Canada (1985) provided the first comprehensive agreement on Pacific salmon and offered a means to cooperate in conservation and development. Unfortunately, it now exemplifies the problem of borders and their risk to biodiversity in Pacific salmon. This talk will address the history of salmon conflicts, the complexity of salmon issues, and describe the risks associated with the present Treaty impasse.

title: Atlantic swordfish management in the 1990's: Will domestic rebuilding be possible in the face of international overfishing?

authors.affiliation: National Marine Fisheries Service, Highly Migratory Species Management Division, F/SF1, 1315 East-West Highway, Silver Spring, MD 20910 USA
National Marine Fisheries Service, Highly Migratory Species Management Division, F/SF1, 1315 East-West Highway, Silver Spring, MD 20910 USA

abstract_text: Atlantic swordfish are a highly migratory species targeted by domestic and international fishing fleets in the North and South Atlantic Oceans. The 22-member International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT) conducts stock assessments and issues management recommendations for swordfish fisheries. In 1996, the North Atlantic swordfish stock was estimated to be at 58% of the biomass needed to produce maximum sustainable yield. In 1997, the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) identified North Atlantic swordfish as overfished and began developing a domestic swordfish rebuilding program under the authority of the Magnuson Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act. This plan may include time/area closures (to limit catch of undersized fish) and import restrictions. In 1997, U.S. swordfish imports totaled more than 15,000 mt and were worth more than US$95 million. As a major importer of swordfish, the U.S. can play a role in international conservation by ensuring that imports are from countries participating in the ICCAT conservation program. NMFS will continue to pursue domestic strategies to rebuild this stock and will work within ICCAT to support international rebuilding strategies. It is not clear what effect restrictions on U.S. fishermen may have in light of increasing international fishing efforts on this highly migratory species.

title: Interstate striped bass management, 1977-1998

authors.affiliation: Virginia Institute of Marine Science, College of William and Mary, Gloucester Point, VA 23062, USA
Virginia Marine Resources Commission, P.O. 756, Newport News, VA 23607, USA

abstract_text: Initially, under the auspices of the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) Interstate Fisheries Management Program, and subsequently the operation of the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission (ASMFC), striped bass (Morone saxatilis) management of the mid-Atlantic (Virginia-Maine) stocks have showed both an initial abysmal beginning, and a final and unique result that can claim responsibility for the dramatic recovery of the heavily fished mid-Atlantic stocks. Recommendations were made to the ASMFC as early as 1942 for the need for more stringent unified regulations that transcended state boundaries; but it was not until 1981 that a Scientific and Statistics Committee recommended to the ASMFC Striped Bass Board that the spawning grounds be closed during the spawning season, and that the minimum size limit be 14" coast-wide; while most of the states adopted such measures in 1982 their enforcement was voluntary. It was not until the passage of the Federal Atlantic Striped Bass Conservation Act in 1984, requiring full compliance with the Act, that each state fulfilled their obligations. Subsequently, a combination of protective regulations and stringent enforcement, coincident with several highly successful dominant year classes (1987, 1989, 1993, and 1996) have led to an unprecedented abundance of large (>24", 600 mm) fish. So successful is the program that Congress has passed subsequent coast-wide legislation (Atlantic Coast Cooperative Fisheries Conservation and Management Act of 1994) to protect other coastal migratory species.

title: Marine turtle movements in the Caribbean: realigning boundaries in the marine environment

authors.affiliation: Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences, University of Florida, 7922 NW 71st Street, Gainesville, Florida 32652 USA

abstract_text: Mitochondrial DNA has proven useful for the elucidation of population structure and questions regarding the behavior of adult female marine turtles. What can the analysis of multiple distinct foraging sites tell us about marine turtle developmental habitats and movements in the Caribbean? Analyses of juvenile foraging populations have provided information regarding recruitment scales in the Caribbean and Atlantic. Previous studies indicate that multiple nesting locations contribute individuals to a particular foraging site. Oftentimes these foraging sites are located outside the geopolitical boundaries of countries supporting the nesting populations. Determination of the composition of juvenile and adult foraging grounds provide information on movement and behavior of marine turtles in the Caribbean and Atlantic. Consequently, this information is necessary for the development of management policies directed towards marine turtles. Migratory behavior of marine organisms forces scientists and management organizations to think differently about how conservation efforts should be directed. Finally, unawareness of human delineated boundaries emphasizes the importance of international cooperation in the maintenance of biodiversity.

title: A bi-national effort to protect endangered Kemp's ridley sea turtles

abstract_text: Hydrogeology of the highly karstic and arid Texas-Mexico border region is complex, and subterranean hydrographic relationships poorly understood, yet these aquifers are heavily exploited for municipal, industrial and agricultural uses. abstract_text: Most often measures of biodiversity have been documented and expressed in regard to political boundaries, as opposed to ecological areas. abstract_text: Forty years ago, Bleakney pointed out that the factors limiting the ranges of herpetofauna had not been well studied. This is still true. abstract_text: At least five species of frogs from North America survive extensive freezing of their body fluids. The roles of physiological systems in the cryobiology of these frogs are varied. Some morphological characteristics and systemic functions are key elements supporting freeze tolerance. For example, the integument transmits ice crystals into body fluids preventing extensive supercooling of body fluids and the cardiovascular system actively distributes cryoprotectant from central stores in the liver to other body tissues before arresting. In contrast, the CNS and skeletal muscle function at temporarily reduced rates upon thawing that are in proportion to the intensity of the freeze episode. This then may affect important organismal activities such as the ability of frogs to find and interact with mates.

Using a cDNA library constructed from liver of wood frogs (Rana sylvatica) frozen for 24 h at -2.5 degrees C, we identified the freeze-induced upregulation of genes coding for the a and S subunits of fibrinogen (a plasma clotting protein), the mitochondrial membrane ADP/ATP translocase, and a novel protein (about 90 amino acids, 10 kD) with a nuclear exporting sequence. title: Evolution of freeze tolerance in turtles: what is known?

abstract_text: Hatchling freeze tolerance has been reported in western painted turtles (NE and various Canadian), midland painted turtles (Ontario and OH), eastern X midland painted turtles (NJ), and ornate box turtles (NE). title: Skirting the edge of hypoxia: overwintering in bullfrogs

abstract_text: It has long been a mystery how aquatically overwintering frogs, such as bullfrogs, survive winter hypoxia. There have been anecdotal reports that frogs bury in mud, but anoxic frogs survived less than two weeks at 4°C in the laboratory, and frogs did not bury in mud when it was available. In the field, while most of the pond bottom was severely hypoxic, the frogs were found in very cold (0-1°) and relatively well oxygenated water at the extreme edge of the pond, centimetres below ice cover. In the laboratory, frogs in a thermal gradient chose colder temperatures when the water was hypoxic (Tattersall and Boutilier; J. Exp. Biol. 200:1031-1038). Frogs have a high Q10 (around 5) below 4°C, thus metabolism is reduced in cold water at the pond edge. Finally, the metabolic rate of overwintering frogs in hypoxic water gradually decreased by 60% over several weeks, reducing fuel consumption and the amount of oxygen required in the water (Donohoe and Boutilier, J. Exp. Biol, in press). Aquatic frogs thus remain aerobic all winter by choosing a low environmental temperature to reduce metabolic rate, choosing water with the highest available oxygen, and reducing metabolic rate at a constant temperature.

abstract_text: Several terrestrial anurans and reptiles that live at high latitudes have developed elaborate physiological and biochemical mechanisms for surviving cold winter temperatures. title: Inter-generic hybrids in emydid turtles, description and possible significance

abstract_text: Hybridization events between species and genera of emydid turtles are rarely reported. Should these hybrids prove to be fertile, crosses will be initiated in order to follow the segregation of traits defining these different Emydid genera.

abstract_text: Blanding's turtles and spotted turtles are listed as Endangered by the state of Indiana. abstract_text: The vermilion snapper (Lutjanidae: Rhomboplites aurorubens) is an important species to commercial and recreational fishers in the southeastern United States, especially in the northern Gulf of Mexico and off the coast of the Carolinas in the South Atlantic Bight (SAB). abstract_text: Histological examination of gonad tissue from 1300 specimens showed that blackbelly rosefish have intraovarian gestation. Fertilization is internal, as free spermatozoa were found primarily in resting ovaries from July through December with peak occurrence in September through November. There was a delay of one to three months before fertilization, as oocyte development did not begin until December. Occurrence during January through April of early-celled embryos, the most advanced stage observed, and postovulatory follicles indicated that oocyte development was rapid. Embryos composed of a blastodermal cap and a large yolk mass were surrounded by a clear gelatinous matrix within the ovary. The reproductive mode in blackbelly rosefish appeared to be intermediate between oviparity and viviparity.

title: Sperm modifications associated with insemination in glandulocaudine fishes

abstract_text: Previous results have demonstrated that females within the subfamily Glandulocaudinae (family Characidae) are inseminated. With the exception of one genus that transfers sperm with spherical nuclei ('aquasperm') to the female, the species of all other genera transfer sperm with elongated nuclei. We have been carrying out transmission electron microscopy on the testes of available species in order to describe the morphology of the mature sperm and to ascertain the mechanisms of nuclear elongation. Additionally, our results have uncovered potential characters that may prove useful in hypothesizing phylogenetic relationships among these taxa. Within the Glandulocaudinae, the mature spermatozoa of the genera Diapoma, Hysteronotus, Corynopoma and Pseudocorynopoma all have the anterior portion of the flagellum contained within an elongated cytoplasmic collar. The mature spermatozoa of Mimagoniates barberi, M. microlepis and M. rheocharis, on the other hand, have very short cytoplasmic collars with the flagellum free along most of its length. However, an analysis of spermiogenesis in these three species showed that during spermatid development, the cytoplasmic collar (containing the flagellum) initially elongates substantially, but subsequently most of the collar degenerates before maturation is complete. Therefore, for the species thus far analyzed, an elongated cytoplasmic collar at least at some point during development may be a synapomorphy.

title: Poecilia formosa, an all-female fish?

abstract_text: Poecilia formosa is known as an all-female species which reproduces gynogenetically. Normally sperm from closely related species trigger the embryogenesis. After breeding Poecilia formosa for 10 years in our laboratory now, we found phenotypic males for the first time last year. The most important question now is whether the masculinized fish are functional Poecilia formosa males which can even reproduce or if they occur because of an error in the development and are therefore only deformed females. To find out the possible effects of these phenotypic males for the whole reproduction complexes, we examined the morphology and the behavior. We could prove that the Poecilia formosa males have a gonopodium, the muscle that moves the gonopodium, a suspensorium and male gonads. With standardized choice experiments we could show that the Poecilia formosa males prefer Poecilia formosa females to Poecilia latipinna females and Poecilia mexicana females. And Poecilia formosa females prefer Poecilia formosa males to Poecilia mexicana males and other Poecilia formosa females. So from the behavior we could expect a normal intraspecific reproduction, as well. On top of these results we got a couple of broods of Poecilia formosa males and Poecilia formosa females since September last year.

title: Reproductive ecology of gulf toadfish (Opsanus beta)

authors.affiliation: University of West Florida, Florida USA
University of West Florida, Florida USA

abstract_text: Gulf toadfish, Opsanus beta, are poorly represented in ecological studies and their reproductive strategies relatively undefined. Our preliminary investigations into breeding seasons and mating behaviors of a Florida gulf toadfish population have revealed several unique and previously undocumented strategies. Ten replicates, each with 5 nest types, were placed in the field and observed from February until November for toadfish activities. Gulf toadfish appear to participate in a bi-peaked breeding season. Males established nests and females oviposit during the month of May, then all fish disappear until late July and breeding resumed in September. Male and female toadfish apparently discriminate between nest types differently. Females preferred nests with one opening over those that are accessible to the surrounding environment through multiple openings. Males, however, showed distinct preferences between the five different nest types based on characteristics of each nest. Males that occupy nests adjacent to other male-occupied nests appear to have greater reproductive success than lone males, contradicting the traditional view that toadfish are highly aggressive and territorial. Male gulf toadfish do not appear to aggressively defend any territory beyond their immediate nest site, an observation which may explain why males in groups experience greater reproductive success.

title: Reproduction of Pseudoplatystoma corruscans (Siluriformes: Pimelodidae) in the Paraná River, State of São Paulo, Brazil

authors.affiliation: Departamento de Educação, UNESP Campus de Assis, SP

abstract_text: Pseudoplatystoma corruscans is a migratory species of economic interest. It is widely distributed in South America (in the basins of the Paraná, San Francisco and Paraguay Rivers) and reproduces in floodplain lagoons where it spends the first phases of its life. Monthly collections, from January 1985 to January 1988, were performed in 150 km of Paraná River, State of São Paulo, Brazil. A total of 255 fish were examined (56% young and 44% adults) measuring between 20.0 and 170.0 cm in total length. Data on body length at first sexual maturation was estimated to be 73.0 cm. This is larger than minimum capture size for this specie determined by the Brazilian Environmental Agency regulating fishing. The reproductive period coincided with the flood period from October to January and schools of mature fish were followed as far as Rio Pardo, a tributary of the Paraná River. In the next months P. corruscans larvae were always collected in marginal ponds. These periodic floods promote the contact of the Paraná River with the marginal ponds and are a requirement to the maintenance of the reproductive processes of P. corruscans.

title: Spatial and temporal patterns of reproductive and trophic divergence in bluegill sunfish

authors.affiliation: Department of Biological Sciences, University of Wisconsin - Milwaukee, 3209 N. Maryland Ave, Milwaukee, WI 53111 USA

abstract_text: A study of bluegill populations from 12 Wisconsin lakes revealed significant differences among lakes in the degree of trophic specialization and sexual dimorphism. Morphological and behavioral variation within and among populations suggested that males compete most intensely for nesting sites in lakes with limited breeding area. Subsequent studies discovered additional bluegill colonies located in deeper areas of lakes for 4 of the most sexually-selected populations. Comparisons between deep-spawning and shallow-spawning colonies showed that deep-spawning bluegill possessed a trophic morphology typical of limnetic specialists and were less sexually dimorphic than bluegill from shallow colonies. Deep- and shallow-spawning bluegill did not differ in mean size or age, however there was greater variation in both age and size among males from the shallow colonies. The relative abundance of cuckolder males was significantly higher in shallow colonies. The mean number of eggs per nest did not differ between colony types, but variation in the number of eggs spawned per nest was greater in the shallow colonies. These data are consistent with the hypothesis that the intensity of sexual selection is greater in the shallow colonies, and that the deep colonies reflect an evolutionary alternative.

title: Morphology and life history of the marine threespine stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus)

authors.affiliation: Dept. of Biology, Clark University, 950 Main St., Worcester, MA 01610, USA

abstract_text: At the close of the last glacial period, only some 15,000 years ago, numerous and varied freshwater aquatic habitats were formed. The threespine stickleback was one of the first fish to colonize these habitats, and these populations have undergone a spectacular adaptive radiation. The threespine stickleback inhabiting nearby coastal marine habitats is the stock from which these freshwater populations were founded. Thus, both the direction and degree of change following freshwater isolation can be inferred by comparing freshwater and marine stickleback. However, the marine form actually may comprise two types: one living and breeding only in marine waters; and a second, anadromous type. At present we know relatively little about whether these types differ in any substantive way. Further, we know little about variation within these types. I present preliminary morphological and life-historical data showing that these types may not be as similar as previously thought, and I compare the level of apparent phenotypic variability with that exhibited by freshwater populations.

title: Evaluating the relationship between organismal trait values and body size, with an example from life-history data for the threespine stickleback, Gasterosteus aculeatus

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, Clark University, Worcester, Massachusetts 01610, USA

abstract_text: The form of the relationship between values for organismal traits (e.g. clutch size) and organism body size has been of interest to biologists for >150 years. This interest has two, somewhat independent foci: to estimate the slope of the relationship itself, and to estimate size-free trait values for comparison across groups. Despite this long interest, there remains considerable controversy over the appropriate statistical model to use in each instance. Most studies use ordinary least squares regression for both, but this is only appropriate when the correlation between the trait of interest and size is quite high (i.e., > 0.9). Such high correlations are infrequent in life-history data sets. Presently, two alternatives for slope estimation appear to be gaining support: major axis regression, and reduced major axis regression. I apply all three methods to a data set for 50 threespine stickleback populations in order to illustrate the considerably different conclusions that can be generated for slopes. Size-adjustment is only appropriately performed using ordinary least squares procedures. Nevertheless, I use a subset of populations to illustrate how faulty conclusions can be generated here, also. No present statistical resolution to this latter problem is apparently in view.

title: Inter- and intra-latitudinal variation in life history traits in migrating silver-phase American eels, Anguilla rostrata

abstract_text: Migrating silver phase American eels were collected from two geographically separated pairs of rivers in Maine. Size at migration, age at migration, mean annular growth, and sex ratios were compared to existing data from other locations to test for the presence of latitudinal changes in life history traits. Comparisons of traits within and among river pairs were also made to examine intra-regional variations. The correlation between latitude and female life history traits resulting from the addition of data from Maine female eels does not support established relationships, reducing the correlation coefficients from 0.64 to 0.28 for length and 0.88 to 0.26 for age. The analysis of male data from Maine eels, however, yields significant correlations between latitude and these traits (size: r=0.94; and age: 0.65). Comparisons of traits among Maine rivers revealed several possible sources of variation that could account for the low relationship between latitude and female traits. Variations observed in these four Maine rivers can be associated with drainage characteristics, methodological differences, and fishing pressure.

title: Phenotypic plasticity in life history traits of Gambusia puncticulata puncticulata (Poeciliidae) from the Cayman Islands, BWI

abstract_text: Gambusia p. puncticulata is a common resident of saline ponds which show high spatio-temporal variability in physico-chemical conditions. We examined variability in reproductive traits of Gambusia p. puncticulata from eight ponds among the three Cayman islands during both rainy and dry periods, in August 1996 and January 1997, respectively. Life-history traits examined included: (1) size at maturity; (2) number of propagules per brood; (3) mean individual weight of propagules; and (4) reproductive allotment. The average standard length of mature males increased significantly between August and January due to the influence of either post-maturation growth or late-maturing males. The mean standard length of mature females was often significantly greater during the dry period than during the wet period. Also, females were nonsuperfetating and provided continual nourishment during propagule development. There was an inverse relationship (r=-.63; n=171) between body-weight adjusted number of propagules and mean individual propagule weight, although both traits increased with somatic weight. This relationship signifies a phenotypic life-history tradeoff. Mean individual propagule weight varied significantly between months and among ponds, whereas reproductive allotment only varied among ponds in Two-Way ANOVAs. Plasticity in life-history traits of these populations may be tied to the dynamic nature of their environment.

abstract_text: Extreme phenotypic plasticity of the lip was discovered in a population of Gambusia hispaniolae during a survey of fishes to Lake Enriquillo, southwestern Dominican Republic, Hispaniola Island. Las Azufradas, a pool of sulfurous water, is tributary to the main lake (Enriquillo). It is the only known habitat for a population of G. hispaniolae characterized by conspicuously enlarged and papillose lower lip that has not been observed in any other member of the genus (although it is superficially similar to the lip of Cyprinodon labiosus, a member of Cyprinodontidae, and also to Poecilia sulphuraria, a member of Poeciliinae). In a sample of more than 200 specimens from Las Azufradas, the enlarged lip was present in 100% of individuals, but no specimen of G. hispaniolae from elsewhere exhibits the character. At the end of the experiment, no differences in lip size or shape were detectable among samples from Las Azufradas and other localities. Feeding habits and effects of food type were also studied. We discuss the possible driving forces that produce the phenotype.
